opener.heading: Week 26: Red, White & Blue Countdown 🎇
about: On Friday Azlyn makes a paper chain with nine links in it, one for every sleep before the Fourth of July, and she tears one off every morning after that. The chain runs the week. Underneath it she builds a drum, a shaker and a flag, marches them down the street, lays a second flag out on the floor from things she carries out of every room, cuts stars she cannot cut, pops paper bags on a countdown she calls herself, and paints a box that stays shut until Sunday. Red, white and blue holds it all together, and the thing she is practicing underneath is waiting for something she can see coming.

Independence Day lands on Sunday the fourth, three days after this week ends, so nothing here is the celebration. Everything is the run-up, which is the part a three-year-old is best at. The other thread is the heat. Late June sets the temperature of every afternoon, so the ice pops, the tub under the sheet and the shaded chalk course are all built around it, and Wednesday moves the whole day out the back door at eight in the morning and leaves it there until dinner.
azlyn: Counting down to a day that has not arrived. Nine links on the wall, one torn off each morning, and a number that gets smaller where she can see it.
Steady beat. Marching in time, feet inside a rhythm her ears are holding, with an instrument in her hands.
Color sorted room by room. Red first, then blue, then white, and she wins every argument about the borderline ones.
Scissor control. Fifty stars drawn fat with room between them, and a hand that works better by the eleventh than the first.
Storytelling with something to lean on. She rolls the cube, says what happens next, and watches you write her words down exactly as they came out.

A sibling's birthday is hard, and preparation helps more than correction

opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 12 months this week. He walks, or is a few steps from it, drinks from a cup he holds himself, and follows a one-step instruction when it is short and he wants to. Every change of surface stops him dead while he works out what his feet are on.

days.title: The Parade Starts Here
days.prepTonight: Cut twenty strips of red, white and blue paper for the chain and tip the recycling onto the table: two cardboard tubes, an empty can, two paper plates.

opening.title: Nine Links Until the Fourth
opening.need: the cut paper strips · 1 glue stick or masking tape · 1 permanent marker.
steps: The red, white and blue strips you cut last night are the countdown chain. Count nine onto the table with her, one for every sleep before the Fourth of July.
Loop the first strip and stick it. Thread the next through and stick that. She sticks, you hold the join.
Hang it where she can reach the bottom link and write 9 on that link. She tears one off each morning. Push the leftover strips aside; the float wants them after lunch.

main.title: Three Instruments and a Flag
materials: 1 empty can or a small saucepan
Red, white and blue paper, or plain paper and markers
1 stick or a second wooden spoon for the flag pole
steps: Shaker first. Tape one end of a tube shut, three strips across and three round the rim. She pours in the half cup of rice. Seal the far end the same way.
Drum next. Lay both paper plates face down over the mouth of the can and tape the rims all the way round. Two plates: one splits inside ten minutes. The wooden spoon is the beater.
Horn last. She hums down the second cardboard tube. Low, high, her own name, Kreston's name.
Cut the fabric scraps and ribbon into eight streamers about a hand long. The scissors are yours.
She tapes the streamers along the top of the stick, then a sheet of red, white and blue paper below them. Plain paper works if she colors it first.
March the hallway three times, once with each instrument, swapping at every turn so nobody keeps the drum.
main.tip: Re-tape the shaker ends after the parade. A tube shaken all morning comes loose at the seam, and half a cup of rice goes across the floor.

outside.title: The Parade Down the Street
paras: Out the front door in a line with the loudest one in front. She picks the route and you walk it at her speed, which stops at every drain cover. Half past ten in late June is warm and not yet hot. Turn at the corner and come back up the other side.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and walking, or close to it. Give him the shaker and let him walk the first stretch with one of your fingers to hold. Carrying while walking is hard work, so he stops every few steps to pick up what he dropped. Put him in the stroller for the way back.

second.title: Kreston's Float
second.intro: The stroller becomes a float this afternoon. At half past two Azlyn takes it up the road with Kreston in it.
materials: The stroller, a wagon, or a large box with a string handle
The morning's instruments and the flag on its pole
1 cushion or folded blanket for the seat
steps: Park the stroller in the middle of the room and let her decide which end is the front.
Clip the leftover paper strips along the hood and down both sides, eight clothespins, and masking tape wherever one has nothing to grip.

Tie the flag pole upright against the handle, the string wound round eight or ten times and knotted twice, so it stands above Kreston's head. If the float is a box, the string is the pull rope: through two holes at the front, knotted no longer than her arm.
Cushion or folded blanket into the seat so he sits high enough to see over the front.
Load him in. Shaker in his hands, drum and horn on Azlyn.
Run the route in the yard or the hall first. She pushes with you, hands on the bar beside yours.
At half past two it goes out the front door and up the road, her hands on the bar and yours beside them the whole way, the brake on at every stop, and you on the curb side.
second.tip: Clip the decorations out of his reach. He will spend the walk pulling at anything within arm's length of the seat.

alternatives: Streamers on the trike or the scooter, and no float at all.
Decorate the front door and stop there.
Load the stroller with teddies and parade them instead.
outAgain: A friend's house, arriving in a parade, so warn them first
The park, one instrument each and the rest left at home
The same street loop again in the cooler part of the afternoon
A neighbor's driveway, if there is one who likes a visit

aroundWorld.title: Independence Days Everywhere 🎇
paras: Plenty of countries mark the day they became their own. Mexico starts on the night of 15 September with el Grito, a shout from a balcony that the whole crowd shouts back. India raises the flag on 15 August and flies kites. Ghana marks 6 March with drumming and school parades.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Lay out a Mexican plate in the flag's three colors: cucumber, white cheese, tomato. Ask Azlyn which country each color belongs to and let her be wrong.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Mexico's celebration begins at eleven o'clock at night, so the children stay up.

days.krestonPM: At 12 months he follows a one-step instruction, so give him one job at the door: give it to Azlyn, with the shaker held out. He hands it over about half the time. Take his shoes off inside and let him walk their floor.

insight.headline: Processions and parades do something specific for children.
paras: Azlyn spends most of her life being moved through the world by adults. A parade hands her the front of the line, a noise nobody tells her to stop making, and a route she chose. Marching also runs on steady beat and steady step, and matching a movement to a rhythm is one of the harder things a three-year-old body does. She is holding a pattern in her ears and putting her feet inside it. Doing that alongside other people, in time with them, is where she builds a lot of her sense of belonging to a group this year.

days.safety: Dried rice in a shaker with a walking 12-month-old who mouths everything: tape both ends shut, check them each time it comes back, and keep the loose rice off the floor. On the street parade she is out front with a drum and not watching the road, so you take the curb side. Knot the pull string short and take it off the box the moment the parade stops.

days.title: Fireworks Without the Bang
days.prepTonight: Cut one end of two cardboard tubes into a fringe with the kitchen scissors, and stand the dark paper, the three paints and a washcloth by the sink.

opening.title: The Black Paper Sky
opening.need: dark blue or black paper, 4 sheets · newspaper · 1 white crayon or a stub of chalk.
steps: Newspaper across the table, then the four dark sheets on top, one at each side so she can walk round them.
Give her the white crayon and ask for the bottom of the sky: rooftops, a fence, trees, whatever she says lives there.
Everything above her line stays empty. Say it is for later and leave all four sheets until 9:15.

main.title: Fireworks Made With a Fork
materials: Dark blue or black paper, 4 sheets (substitute: a cereal box painted dark)
Washable non-toxic poster paint in red, white and blue
2 cardboard tubes, one end cut into a fringe
steps: Newspaper back down. Red and white onto one shallow plate, blue onto the other, wet washcloth in its bowl at her elbow.
Press the back of the fork into the paint, then straight down onto the dark paper and straight up again. Turn a quarter, press again round the same middle. Four presses make one burst.
Whisk next. Dip the round underside, press, hold for a count of two. It prints fatter than the fork.
Fringed tube last. Dip the cut end, press, twist a quarter turn before lifting.
Let her fill all four sheets and go on filling them. Hands into the washcloth between colors or the sky turns purple.
Lay them flat on the floor out of Kreston's line to dry. She comes back at 4:15.
main.tip: Load the fork light. A fork thick with paint prints a blob, and a fork with almost nothing on it prints thin lines that read as a firework.

outside.title: Flowers Shaped Like Fireworks
paras: Late June is the two weeks for this. Look for flowers that burst out of one point: alliums on their tall stalks, the domed head on a milkweed, Queen Anne's lace on the roadside, a dandelion clock gone to seed. Get her to trace one from the middle out to the tip, then bring a clock home and blow it on the doorstep. Leave the milkweed stem unbroken, because the white sap inside it stings eyes.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and everything in his hand travels to his mouth. Sit him at the far end of the table with the wet washcloth and let him press it onto the newspaper, where it leaves a dark mark that fades while he watches. He will do that twenty times. On the walk he pushes the stroller along one flat stretch.

second.title: The Bang She Controls
second.intro: A firework goes off whether or not she is ready. Every loud noise this afternoon starts with her hands, and she counts it down first.
materials: 1 folded towel to muffle the floor
steps: Set up at the far end of the room from Kreston, or hand him over and take this hour with her alone. Everything happens on the folded towel.
Bags first. She blows one up, twists the neck, and you both count backwards from three before she claps it flat. Six bags, six goes, all hers.
Pop the second bag under a cushion so she hears how much it takes away. The other cushion is hers, for her ears.
Saucepan on the towel, lid in her hands. Lid on pan, lid on towel, wooden spoon on pan. Three sounds, and she names each one.
Bubble wrap flat on the towel. Stamp along it, then roll it up and squeeze with both arms.
Second round is hers to order. She says what is coming, you both count, and she does it.
Finish on the floor with the towel over the bubble wrap. Ask her which was loudest.
second.tip: Say the noise out loud before it arrives, every time, in the same words. Ready. Three, two, one, bang. She will start doing the countdown herself.

alternatives: Bubble wrap only, on the hall floor, in socks.
Drum on upturned pans in the yard where the sound has somewhere to go.
Blow the bags up and let them go without popping any.
outAgain: The botanical garden, still hunting flowers built like fireworks
The park, with the shadiest bench you know
A quiet walk with the stroller if the afternoon has been loud enough
The garden center, cool inside and full of the same flower shapes
days.krestonPM: Take him round the botanical garden on foot. At 12 months he stops at every edge, every step and every change of surface, and gravel to grass to path is the whole outing to him. Let him drink from his cup on a bench in the shade.

insight.headline: Children take their fear reading from your face first.
paras: A loud unexpected noise sends Azlyn's eyes to you before she decides anything about it. Psychologists call the habit social referencing, and it is running hard in both of them this year. Your face is the fastest information available and she trusts it over her own ears. This is why the countdown works: she gets the warning, she watches you stay unbothered, and the bang arrives inside a frame she already has. Firework night in eight days will be easier for the same reason. Name the noise before it comes, keep your shoulders down, and she borrows your reading of it.

days.safety: A saucepan lid banged near Kreston's head is loud enough to hurt him at 12 months. Keep every bang at the far end of the room from him, or take him out for the ten loudest minutes. Washable non-toxic paint only this morning, and expect him to put a painted hand in his mouth.

days.title: Red, White and Frozen
days.prepTonight: Clear a flat shelf in the freezer wide enough for eight paper cups standing up, and move the yogurt, the juice and the fruit to the front of the fridge.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Coolest Spot on the Street

opening.title: Mashing the Blueberries
opening.need: the pint of blueberries · 1 fork · 1 pitcher.
steps: Tip the pint into the pitcher and hand her the fork. Mashing blueberries takes longer than she expects, which is why it belongs at 8:00.
Stand the pitcher in the fridge. This is the top layer and it waits until late morning.
Give her the last few whole ones to eat.

main.title: The Three-Layer Ice Pops
materials: Blueberries, one pint, or grape juice
8 craft sticks or plastic spoons for the handles
1 teaspoon or plastic spoon for the yogurt
steps: Hull the strawberries, two or three into each of the eight paper cups. She squashes them with the fork and pours about 100 ml of juice between the eight.
Stand the cups in the corner of the freezer shelf where they cannot tip. They want an hour.
At the 10:15 snack they come out. She spoons yogurt over the frozen red with a plastic spoon, a heaped load per cup.
Tear eight squares of kitchen foil. Press one over each cup and push a craft stick through the middle into the yogurt, which holds it standing.
Before lunch, stir the last 200 ml of juice into the mashed blueberries. Lift each foil square, pour the blue on top and press the foil back down.
At 3:30, run one cup under the warm tap for three seconds and peel the paper off in one piece.
main.tip: She will want one at eleven. Take her to the freezer, let her look at the half-frozen cups and put them back herself.

outside.title: The Coolest Spot on the Street
paras: Go out hunting shade and be home before the sun is overhead. Name what makes each patch of it: the north side of a wall, the big tree, a parked van, a deep doorway. Ask her which of them will still be shaded when you come past on the way home this afternoon, and chalk a mark on the sidewalk at the two she picks. Then stand in the deepest one for a minute with your eyes shut and let her tell you what she can hear.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and drinks from a cup, so his water goes everywhere you go today and he gets offered it whether or not he asks. He walks the shaded stretches and rides the sunny ones. A hat stays on him for about four minutes, so take the stroller with the hood up.

second.title: The Tub Under the Sheet
second.intro: One old sheet over the clothesline makes a room with shade in it, and the tub goes underneath.
materials: The clothesline, or two chairs and a broom handle
steps: Clip the old sheet along the clothesline with the six clothespins, one edge low, so the shade falls where you sit. Two chairs and the broom handle across their backs do the same job.
Set the dishpan in that shade and fill it a hand's depth with cold water. No deeper, today or any other day.
Spread one towel where she kneels and keep the second folded within reach.
In go the two pitchers, the four cups, the sieve and the sponge. Show her one thing, pouring from high so it splashes, then stop.
The sieve holds her longest, because water leaves it and she cannot see where it went.
The sponge goes in last: fill, lift, squeeze over her own knees, and half the tub ends up on the grass.
Drinking water stands in the shade beside you and both of them drink at the top of every hour. When she has finished, tip the bowl out and turn it over.
second.tip: Refill the bowl twice rather than filling it deep. Shallow water warms up, which she prefers, and the depth never changes.

alternatives: Wash the dolls in the bowl and clip them on the line to dry.
One pitcher and the doorstep, no tub at all.
Paint the fence with water and a decorating brush.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks, late enough that the water has the shade
The kiddie pool at the park if the town has one
A shaded woodland path where the temperature drops as you walk in
The library, for the air conditioning as much as the books
days.krestonPM: He sits beside the bowl, never in it and never on his own. At 12 months he tips a cup over on purpose to watch what comes out, so give him one of his own on the towel away from the tub. Watch his feet on hot paving now that he walks barefoot.

insight.headline: Heat, hunger, and tiredness account for most "bad behavior."
paras: A late June afternoon does more to Azlyn's mood than anything you say to her. Small bodies heat up faster than yours and cool down slower, and a three-year-old cannot read the signal or name it. She gets a meltdown over a cup instead. Before you deal with the behavior, run the three: has she drunk anything in the last hour, has she eaten since lunch, has she been out in the sun without a hat. Fix whichever one is missing and most of the trouble goes with it. The afternoons that need managing are the afternoons that needed a glass of water an hour earlier.

days.safety: A 12-month-old drowns in the depth of water that is in that tub. Kreston never sits beside it unwatched, and you tip it out the moment you go in, not later. Late June sun: hats, sunscreen on both of them before you go out and again after lunch, shade by 11:00, and check the tub water and any metal or dark plastic with your own hand before either child touches it.

days.title: Roll, Then Tell
days.prepTonight: Find a small square box, a tissue box or a cube-shaped parcel box, and stand it on the table with the permanent marker and the masking tape.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Whatever Happens at the Next Corner

opening.title: Drawing on All Six Sides
opening.need: the small square box · 1 permanent marker · 1 roll masking tape.
steps: Tape the box shut on every open edge so it holds its shape when it lands.
Ask her for six things: a person, an animal, a place, a weather, a food, and one of her own choosing. Draw each on a face while she watches. Yours will not be good and she will tell you so.
Roll it across the floor once. Whatever lands on top, name it out loud. Then it sits in the middle of the table until 9:15.

main.title: The Story the Dice Tells
materials: 1 small square box, a tissue box or a cube-shaped parcel box
steps: Sit on the floor with the paper and the pen beside you. Write Once there was at the top of the first sheet and let her finish the sentence out loud.
She rolls the cube. Whatever is on top is the next thing that happens in the story, and she says how.
Write her words down as they come. No tidying, no fixing the grammar, no better version of what she meant.
Roll again. Six or seven rolls is a whole story, and the same picture landing twice means it comes back.
If a face has stopped working for her, tape a fresh square of paper over it and draw something new with the permanent marker. She chooses what.
Read the finished thing back to her, out loud, at full commitment, in her exact words.
main.tip: A three-year-old's plot has a dog, then a cake, then the dog again, and you read it back with a straight face.

outside.title: Whatever Happens at the Next Corner
paras: At every corner she calls left or right and you go that way without comment. Between corners, narrate what you pass as if it were the story: the cat on the wall wanted something, the parked van has been there since Friday. Late June mornings are warm by eleven, so take the shady side home.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and follows a one-step instruction. Roll the cube toward him and say bring it, and about half the time he will. Carrying an object across a room to another person is what he practices hardest this month, and the box is light enough for both hands.

second.title: Six Pages and a Cover
second.intro: Her story exists on four loose sheets in your handwriting. This afternoon it becomes a book.
materials: Plain paper, 4 sheets, folded in half
1 roll masking tape for the spine
steps: Fold the four sheets in half, stack them one inside another, and run masking tape down the outside of the fold. That is a cover and six pages, with a couple spare.
Read the story back and stop at each thing that happens. One thing, one page. Number them with the permanent marker while she watches.
Crayons out. She draws page one, and you say nothing about what it looks like and add nothing to it.
Write her sentence for that page underneath the drawing, word for word, the same as this morning.
Keep going. Six pages if she stays, three pages if she does not, and three pages is a book.
Cover last. She chooses the title and you write it, then she does her own name however her name comes out.
Sit Kreston down and let her read it to him. She will not read the words, and it does not matter.
second.tip: Put the date on the back cover in permanent marker before it goes on the shelf. In two years the handwriting will be the interesting part and neither of you will remember which June this was.

alternatives: One page, one drawing, and call it finished.
Act the story out with teddies instead of drawing it.
Draw the story on one long strip of paper end to end.
Tell a second story with the cube and write nothing down.
outAgain: The neighborhood park, with the cube in your pocket for a story on the bench
The same corner-by-corner walk, going the other way this time
The green space with a ball
A shaded bit of woodland, with her book to read under a tree
The playground with the big slide, late enough that the metal has cooled
days.krestonPM: At 12 months he listens to Azlyn read for about ninety seconds and then wants the book itself. Let him have it once she has finished, and expect a bent corner. At the park he walks the flat path and pulls himself up the first step of the climbing frame. Stay a hand's width behind him.

insight.headline: Storytelling with prompts is easier than storytelling from nothing.
paras: Ask Azlyn to tell you a story and she freezes or recites a movie. Hand her a picture that has already landed and she is away. The hard part of storytelling at three is the choosing: settling on what comes next out of everything that could come next, while also finding the words for it. The cube does the choosing and leaves her the connecting. A prompt gets longer sentences out of her than a blank start does, and more complicated ones. Writing her words down without editing them tells her the sentences were worth keeping, and she notices that.

days.safety: The permanent marker and its cap go back on the table out of Kreston's reach the moment you stop writing, at 8:00 and again over the book. Everything else on the floor is his: check the cube for loose tape before you roll it to him, and pick the masking tape and the offcuts up as you go. On the corner walk you take the curb side. The turn is hers and the road is yours, at every corner, including the ones where she has already set off.

days.title: The Flag on the Floor
days.prepTonight: Empty the laundry basket and stand it by the stairs, and put a white sheet or a big bath towel on the arm of the sofa.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Every Red Thing She Can Carry

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Flag Made of Things From the House

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Flat on Our Backs in the Grass

opening.title: Every Red Thing She Can Carry
opening.need: 1 laundry basket · her · one room at a time.
steps: Give her the basket and one word: red. Start in her bedroom and do not help her choose.
Follow her round. Name each thing as it goes in, and let the arguable ones in; orange counts if she says it counts.
Stop when the basket is heavy enough that she has to drag it. Tip nothing out; it comes to the front room at 9:15.

main.title: The Flag Made of Things From the House
materials: 1 white sheet or bath towel as the base
Red, white and blue objects from around the house
steps: Spread the sheet on the floor in the room with the best light and smooth the creases with her.
The red things from 8:00 go down first, in a long line across the bottom edge. Leave a stripe of bare sheet, then another red line above it. Four or five stripes with white sheet between them.
Send her out for blue, one room at a time. Blue fills a square in the top left corner, packed as solid as she can get it.
White goes last, on the blue, one white thing for each star. Buttons are out, so think socks, paper, a plastic spoon, a hair clip too big to swallow.
Hold the phone as high over it as your arm reaches and take the photograph. Let her take one at her height, and keep both.
Everything goes back in the basket the way it came out, her job at 4:00.
main.tip: Do not straighten her stripes. She carries a wonky flag she laid herself back to every room this afternoon, telling you where each thing lives.

outside.title: Flat on Our Backs in the Grass
paras: Take a rug to the shadiest grass you can reach and lie on your backs, all three of you. Late June skies at eleven are full of movement: swifts, a plane, a seed head, one cloud with an edge on it. Say what you can see, let her say what she can see, and stay down longer than feels reasonable.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and walking, which makes the flag on the floor a road. Give him three white things of his own on the far side of the sheet, each one too big for his mouth: a folded pillowcase, a plastic mixing bowl, a paper plate. Let him walk to them. Lying on his back in the grass is a harder ask now that he can stand, so put him beside Azlyn and let him crawl off when he has had enough.

second.title: Fifty Stars Is a Lot
second.intro: The flag has fifty stars and Azlyn cuts every one she can face. Stopping at eleven is fine.
materials: Blue card or paper, 2 sheets (substitute: white paper colored in)
1 glue stick, or flour-and-water paste in a saucer
steps: Draw ten stars on each sheet of white paper with the marker. Big ones, fat points, room between them.
Hand her the child scissors and let her cut them out. They will not come out as stars. Every one goes on the flag anyway.
Lay the two blue sheets side by side. With no blue in the house she colors two white sheets in with the marker, ten minutes she enjoys.
Glue stick, or a spoonful of flour-and-water paste in the saucer that she spreads with one finger. The paste is slower and she will pick it.
She sticks them down and counts out loud as she goes. Count with her, then count again when she has finished, because the two numbers will not match.
Write the real number on the back with the marker and the date beside it.
Cutting is tiring. When she puts the scissors down, that is the end of it.
second.tip: Cut two or three yourself at the start so she has something to compare against, then stop. Fifteen minutes in she is cutting to cut and the stars have stopped mattering.

alternatives: Tear the stars instead of cutting them.
Stick the stars on the window with tape instead of on card.
Count fifty of anything: pasta, socks, steps up the road.
outAgain: Swimming, and the pool is the coolest room in town this week
The splash pad if the pool is packed with the holiday crowd
A shaded park and a bottle of water each
Indoor playground with the air conditioning on
days.krestonPM: He goes in the water too. At 12 months he can stand in the shallow end holding both your hands and take steps against the drag, which is hard work and he loves it. Twenty-five minutes is plenty. Get him out while he is enjoying it and feed him within the half hour.

insight.headline: Sorting by one property at a time is how a category gets built.
paras: Carrying a basket room by room with one word in her head, red, is a harder job than it looks. She has to hold the rule while everything in the room competes for it: the toy she wants, the sock under the bed, the book she started on Sunday. Psychologists call the holding part selective attention, and at three it runs on one property at a time. Color holds her longer than shape or size, so it makes the best first rule. Let the arguable ones in. Orange counting as red tells you she has a rule of her own and is applying it, and the rule matters more this year than the sorting.

days.safety: She is collecting small objects from every room and laying them at floor height while Kreston walks around them. Coins, magnets, buttons and anything holding a button battery go straight back in the basket, not on the sheet. Sweep the line she works along before you put him down. Late June sun reaches her on a shaded rug, so hats and sunscreen on both of them before you go out. At the pool both of them stay inside arm's reach in the water, close enough to take hold of without a step, and armbands and rings are toys rather than supervision. The child scissors live on the table and go back in the drawer the moment she leaves it. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Whole Day Outside
days.prepTonight: Fill two pitchers with water and put them in the fridge, and pile by the back door what the day needs: the old sheet, the markers, the string, the clothespins, the chalk, a shallow dish for the birds.

schedule.name: The Course She Sets Out Herself

opening.title: Everything Goes Out the Back Door
opening.need: the pile by the back door · 1 laundry basket · 1 rug or picnic blanket.
steps: Tell her the plan before she asks: today the table is outside and it stays out until dinner.

The pile by the back door is the day's kit: the old sheet, the markers, the string, the clothespins, the chalk and the shallow dish for the birds. Load it into the basket together and let her carry it out in as many trips as she wants. Trips are the activity.
Spread the rug in the shade the house casts at 8:00, and say the shade will move and so will the rug.

main.title: Twenty Flags on a String
materials: 1 old sheet, or 6 paper grocery bags
Red and blue markers, or washable paint and a brush
steps: Cut twenty triangles from the old sheet or the paper bags, a hand span along the top edge. You cut, she counts them into a pile and says when there are twenty.
Red and blue markers, or the paint and brush if you want it wetter. She covers as many as she wants and leaves the rest plain.
Write on four with the permanent marker: her name, Kreston's, yours, Joseph's. She says which flag belongs to whom.
Tie the string between two fixed points, four meters of it, high enough that she walks under it with a hand up.
Fold the top edge of each triangle over the string and clip it. One clothespin pinches two neighbors together, so twelve of them hold twenty flags.
Stand at one end and count along the line with her, out loud, to twenty.
main.tip: Cut all twenty before she starts coloring. A three-year-old colors four flags with enormous care and the last sixteen in a single stroke each.

outside.title: Water Out for the Birds
paras: The last day of June is hot and every bird on the street is hunting for water. Set a shallow dish in the shade of the wall, no deeper than her thumb, with one stone standing proud in the middle so a bee can land on it and climb out again. She fills it from the pitcher and marks the level on the outside with chalk. Walk the block while it settles, counting the birds you hear rather than the ones you see, and check the mark against the water when you get back.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and a new walker, so a change of surface stops him dead while he works out what his feet are standing on. Give him his own cup of water to carry as far as the dish, which is one instruction and a job he can finish. Most of it lands on his feet, and he will go back for the rest.

second.title: The Course She Sets Out Herself
second.intro: Ninety minutes of running about in the heat needs shape or it turns into whining. Azlyn draws the shape herself and you follow it.
materials: 1 plank or a long strip of flattened cardboard
3 of the morning's flags as station markers
steps: Hand her the chalk and two fixed points: the course starts at the back door and ends wherever she says.
She draws the line. Walk behind her and mark nothing yourself, including the bit that goes through the flower bed.
Set the stations where her line passes them. Two buckets to step in and out of, the plank to walk along, three cushions spaced for jumping between.
Tuck one of the morning's flags under each of the three stations so she sees them from the start line.
Run it together, counting out loud, and tell her the number at the end. She will want to beat it.
The pitcher of water and the cups live at the middle station. She drinks a full cup every time she passes it, and so does Kreston.
She changes the course whenever she likes. A wet foot rubs the chalk out and she redraws it somewhere worse.
second.tip: Move the course into shade after one o'clock rather than shortening it. Chalk redraws in two minutes and the cushions carry.

alternatives: One plank and one bucket, and nothing else.
Chalk a hopscotch grid on the paving instead.
Draw round all three of you on the paving and color the outlines in.
outAgain: Indoor playground, indoors and cool, on the hottest afternoon of the week
The shaded end of the park, later than usual
The splash pad or the kiddie pool
A cool store with wide aisles, and let her push the basket
days.krestonPM: Indoor playground is a different building for him now that he walks. At 12 months he goes into the baby area and out of it under his own steam, and the ball pit is work rather than fun because the floor moves. Ten minutes of the padded slope on his feet, holding your hands. Water and a sit-down after twenty minutes.

insight.headline: Outdoor play is the highest-return activity available, and June is when it gets easy.
paras: A day like this buys you more than any indoor plan. Outdoors, Azlyn runs faster, talks more, argues less and sleeps better that night, and the space does the work you would be doing with instructions. Daylight sets her body clock, and you collect that at bedtime. Uneven ground builds balance no flat floor can teach her. Her eyes spend the whole day focusing at distance, and the research linking outdoor hours to lower rates of nearsightedness is strong enough to act on. From here to September the barrier is low: open the door, carry the water out, and let the garden run the day.

days.safety: A whole day outdoors at the end of June is a heat day. Water at every station and not only when she asks, hats on, sunscreen on both of them before you open the door and again after lunch, and the middle of the day spent in shade. Test the plank, the buckets and any dark surface with your own hand first, and watch Kreston's feet on hot paving now that he is walking. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Someone Else's Birthday
days.prepTonight: Flatten a large cardboard box down one side so it opens out, stand it by the back door with the packing tape, and gather the week's makes into one pile.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Setting the Table Three Days Early

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Every Flag Between Here and the Corner

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Box That Waits Until Sunday

opening.title: Three Links Left
steps: The paper chain on the wall counts the sleeps left before the Fourth of July. She tears off today's link and holds the chain up. Three left, and she can see all three at once now.
Count them with her: Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Say what happens on each, in order, the same way every morning from here.
Write 3 on the bottom link and hang it back up. Leave the question of whose birthday it is for the Morning Meeting.

main.title: Setting the Table Three Days Early
materials: Paper plates and cups, one per person
A tablecloth or an old sheet
steps: The tablecloth or the old sheet goes on first and she smooths it flat with both arms.
Tape a length of the week's bunting along the front edge so it hangs where she can see it from her chair, and lay the flags down the middle.
Count the people in the house out loud on fingers. One paper plate and one paper cup each, and she carries them over one at a time.
Write each name on a cup with the permanent marker. She tells you whose is whose, then adds her own marks to each one.
She decides who sits where. Take her seating plan as final, including the part where Kreston sits next to her.
Fill the cups from the pitcher of water and eat the 10:15 snack sitting at it, in the right seats, three days early.
main.tip: Leave it set. She will walk past a table that stays laid and rearrange it eleven times before Sunday.

outside.title: Every Flag Between Here and the Corner
paras: The flags go up on houses this week, so walk the street and count them. Front porches, cars, a sticker in a window, bunting over a driveway. She counts and you keep the running total. Go as far as the corner and decide together whether the next street has more.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and sits at the table in his own seat with a paper cup he can lift himself. Half of it goes down his front and the other half gets drunk, and both count as practice. Give him a paper plate of his own at the snack. At the table he watches Azlyn hard, and copying her does more for him than anything you demonstrate.

second.title: The Box That Waits Until Sunday
second.intro: Most of what the week made goes into one box this afternoon. She paints it, prints her hand on the side, and it is shut until Sunday.
materials: Washable non-toxic paint in red, white and blue
The week's makes: the instruments, the star field, her book
steps: Box out on the grass, paint beside it, and she goes at the outside with the wide brush. No plan, no design, all four sides and the flaps.

Handprint next. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand, press it flat on the front, count to three and lift straight up. Do Kreston's beside hers if he will hold his fingers open for a second. Write JULY and 3 beside the two of them.
Wet washcloth straight away, both sets of hands, before either of them gets to a face or the door handle.

Load it while the paint dries: the instruments, the star field, her book. The chain stays on the wall, because there are two more links to tear before the box opens, and the flags and the bunting stay on the table she laid this morning. Photograph each thing as it goes in, because the box gets emptied in a hurry on Sunday.
She puts the last thing in and closes the flaps herself.
Packing tape across the seam. You write OPEN JULY 4 on the top in permanent marker and she goes over your letters with her own hand on the marker.
Up on top of the closet now, not at bedtime.
second.tip: Keep her book out if she asks for it. Three days is a long time to a three-year-old.

alternatives: Paint the box and leave it empty until Saturday.
Skip the paint and let her cover the box in stickers and marker.
Make a birthday card for the country and post it on the fridge.
outAgain: The hardware store, for a packet of flag stakes or a length of rope for Sunday
The grocery store, and she picks one thing for the Fourth
The park on the shaded side, with the cube in your pocket
The bakery, for something to eat at the table she laid
days.krestonPM: The hardware store at 12 months is a corridor of things at his own height. Put him in the cart seat for the aisles and let him walk the wide empty bit by the registers. Give him one thing too big for his mouth to hold the whole way round, and he will keep it.

insight.headline: A sibling's birthday is hard, and preparation helps more than correction.
paras: Sunday is a party for somebody who is not Azlyn, and a three-year-old does not separate a country's birthday from her own the way you do. She will ask where her cake is. Telling her on the day that it is not about her lands as a correction, and she has done nothing wrong. Telling her three days early, at a table she laid herself, gives her a job inside the celebration instead. The same thing works for Kreston's next birthday: a role, a task, something of her own to carry. Preparation gets you a helper, and correction gets you a scene.

days.safety: The box fills up with the rice shaker and the drum beater at exactly Kreston's height, and at 12 months he helps himself to open boxes. Tape it shut and put it up high the moment you finish, not at bedtime. Washable non-toxic paint only, and wipe his hands before he touches his face.
